note: Fact records for the boards hub. Schema and rules: src/boards/facts/README.md. Quotes are verified by tools/boards/check-quotes.mjs.

facts.claim: The 2008 AAE consensus conference produced 13 diagnostic terms: 7 pulpal and 6 periapical. Pulpal: normal pulp, reversible pulpitis, symptomatic irreversible pulpitis, asymptomatic irreversible pulpitis, pulp necrosis, previously treated, previously initiated therapy. Apical: normal apical tissues, symptomatic apical periodontitis, asymptomatic apical periodontitis, acute apical abscess, chronic apical abscess, condensing osteitis.

cites.quote: 13 diagnostic terms to describe the different pulpal (seven terms) and periapical (six terms) conditions

facts.claim: Normal pulp: symptom-free and responds normally to pulp testing; a cold response is felt but fades within about 1-2 seconds.
facts.conditions: The normal-pulp '1-2 seconds' figure was not found in the fetched text (BDJ table cells); the quote here is the contrasting irreversible-pulpitis cell. Don't key the exact seconds for a normal pulp.

cites.quote: Sharp pain on stimulation, lasting >30 seconds

facts.claim: Reversible pulpitis: inflammation expected to resolve once the cause (e.g., caries) is removed; no spontaneous pain; cold/sweet discomfort that fades quickly; no percussion tenderness; no apical radiographic change.

cites.quote: indicating that the inflammation should resolve and the pulp return to ‘normal’

facts.claim: Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis: vital, inflamed pulp that cannot heal; descriptors are lingering thermal pain, spontaneous pain and referred pain. BDJ 2025 operationalizes "lingering" as thermal pain lasting more than 30 seconds; EPT usually still positive; percussion pain in some cases.

cites.quote: Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis A clinical diagnosis based on subjective (lingering pain to thermal changes for extended period)
lingering thermal pain, spontaneous pain and referred pain
Sharp pain on stimulation, lasting >30 seconds

facts.claim: Asymptomatic irreversible pulpitis: vital, inflamed pulp that cannot heal but with no symptoms and normal thermal responses; the clue is objective, e.g., deep caries or fracture encroaching on the pulp.

cites.quote: Asymptomatic irreversible Pulpitis A clinical diagnosis based on subjective (no clinical symptoms and responses to thermal testing are within normal limits)

facts.claim: Pulp necrosis: no response to sensibility testing; may carry an apical diagnosis.

cites.quote: Pulp necrosis A necrotic pulp No pulp symptoms reported but may have associated apical symptoms and diagnosis Non-responsive to sensibility testing

facts.claim: Previously treated = canals already obturated (with materials other than intracanal medicaments). Previously initiated therapy = partial endodontic therapy already done (e.g., pulpotomy, pulpectomy, access).

cites.quote: is a clinical diagnostic category indicating that the tooth has been previously treated by partial endodontic therapy ( e.g. , pulpotomy, pulpectomy)

facts.claim: Normal apical tissues: not sensitive to percussion or palpation; intact lamina dura and uniform PDL space.
facts.conditions: Normal apical tissues (no percussion or palpation tenderness, intact lamina dura, uniform PDL) is from BDJ Table 1, which the fetched text doesn't carry as a clean cell; quote pending.

cites.quote: the lamina dura surrounding the root is intact and the periodontal ligament space is uniform

facts.claim: Symptomatic apical periodontitis: apical inflammation of pulpal origin with a painful response to biting and/or percussion or palpation; a radiolucency may or may not be present.

cites.quote: producing clinical symptoms including a painful response to biting and/or percussion or palpation. It might or might not be associated with an apical radiolucent area

facts.claim: Asymptomatic apical periodontitis: apical inflammation and destruction of pulpal origin that shows as an apical radiolucency and causes no clinical symptoms.

cites.quote: appears as an apical radiolucent area, and does not produce clinical symptoms

facts.claim: Acute apical abscess: rapid onset, spontaneous pain, tooth tender to pressure, pus and swelling. Chronic apical abscess: gradual onset, little or no discomfort, intermittent pus discharge through a sinus tract.

cites.quote: characterized by rapid onset, spontaneous pain, tenderness of the tooth to pressure, pus formation and swelling of as
characterized by gradual onset, little or no discomfort and the intermittent discharge of pus through an associated sinus tract

facts.claim: Condensing osteitis: diffuse radiopaque lesion at or around the root apex, a localized bone reaction to a low-grade inflammatory stimulus.

cites.quote: Condensing osteitis Diffuse radiopaque lesion representing a localized bony reaction to a low‐grade inflammatory stimulus, usually seen at apex

facts.claim: Thermal (cold) response separates the pulpal categories: normal and reversible = brief response that resolves; symptomatic irreversible = lingering pain; necrosis = no response.

cites.quote: Sharp pain on stimulation, lasting >30 seconds

facts.claim: Percussion/bite tenderness points to the apical diagnosis (symptomatic apical periodontitis), not the pulp diagnosis; a radiolucency with no tenderness = asymptomatic apical periodontitis; a sinus tract = chronic apical abscess; swelling with rapid onset = acute apical abscess.

cites.quote: a painful response to biting and/or percussion or palpation
intermittent discharge of pus through an associated sinus tract

facts.claim: Endodontic diagnosis is stated as a pulpal diagnosis and an apical (periapical) diagnosis for the tooth.

cites.quote: The pulp and periapical diagnosis of a tooth determines to a great extent the course of endodontic treatment

facts.claim: Teeth that are calcified, traumatized, irradiated or had vital pulp therapy may not respond to pulp testing without being necrotic; IEJ 2022 proposes an "inconclusive pulp condition" term for them (a proposal, not current AAE terminology).
facts.conditions: 'Inconclusive pulp condition' is the IEJ 2022 authors' proposal, not AAE terminology: never key it as an AAE diagnosis.

cites.quote: Inconclusive pulp condition A clinical diagnostic category in which the pulp is symptom‐free and is not responding normally to pulp testing

facts.claim: Cold refrigerant thresholds, EPT interpretation in immature teeth, and exact cracked-tooth bite-test wording are technique details that require source-specific review.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked. The cited review documents limitations of sensibility testing but does not establish a universal refrigerant temperature or EPT threshold; do not key those values.

facts.claim: Cold and electric pulp tests are sensibility tests: they infer pulp status from a sensory nerve response and do not directly demonstrate pulp blood flow.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; the automated quote check confirms wording only. Sensibility is not the same as histologic diagnosis or a direct vitality measurement.

facts.claim: Pulp vitality testing aims to assess blood flow; laser Doppler flowmetry and pulse oximetry are examples, but they have practical limits and have not displaced sensibility tests as routine clinical tests.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; this describes the review's evidence at publication, not a current device-specific recommendation.

facts.claim: A necrotic, infected canal is poorly reached by systemic antibiotics because the pulp tissue is no longer vascularized; local canal debridement addresses the source.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; do not extend this to all odontogenic infections or to trauma prophylaxis.

facts.claim: Early apical inflammation may produce periodontal ligament changes before a periapical radiolucency is visible; a normal image does not exclude symptomatic apical periodontitis.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; radiographic visibility depends on lesion stage, projection and anatomy.

cites.quote: there may be normal width of the periodontal ligament

facts.claim: Pain history should record onset, duration, location, triggers, relief, referral, prior treatment and medications before the clinical tests are interpreted.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; patient descriptions can be imprecise and must be reconciled with examination findings.

facts.claim: Test adjacent and contralateral teeth first to give the patient a comparison for normal cold and percussion responses.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; use clinically comparable control teeth and interpret results with the full exam.

facts.claim: Cold testing applies a thermal stimulus and records whether the patient senses it and how long the response persists; it tests sensory response, not blood flow.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; technique, restoration coverage and patient response affect interpretation.

facts.claim: EPT elicits a sensory response but does not distinguish a healthy pulp from an inflamed one by itself; false positive responses can result when current reaches gingiva or adjacent teeth.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; use isolation and compare with control teeth; EPT is not a stand-alone diagnosis.

facts.claim: A recently traumatized or calcified tooth can fail to respond to sensibility testing despite retained pulp vitality; one negative test alone does not establish necrosis.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; trauma follow-up requires serial clinical and radiographic review.

facts.claim: Percussion and palpation test response of the apical tissues, not pulp sensibility; a painful response can support symptomatic apical periodontitis.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; percussion tenderness is not specific to endodontic disease and requires a differential diagnosis.

facts.claim: A cusp-by-cusp bite test can reproduce pain associated with a crack; it helps localize symptoms but does not alone prove crack depth or pulp status.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; use with transillumination, magnification, probing and radiographs as indicated.

facts.claim: Endodontic imaging commonly uses periapical views from more than one angle; bitewings can help assess coronal disease, while CBCT is reserved for cases where conventional imaging does not answer a clinical question.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; use the smallest field of view and justified imaging selection; this is not a routine CBCT indication.

facts.claim: AAE normal pulp is symptom-free and normally responsive to pulp tests; a brief cold response that stops after stimulus removal is typical.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; normal is a clinical category and does not assert histologically normal tissue.

facts.claim: Reversible pulpitis causes stimulus-evoked discomfort, commonly to cold or sweet, that stops quickly; spontaneous pain and significant periapical radiographic change are not typical.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; reassess after the cause is managed because the diagnosis may change.

cites.quote: goes away within a couple of seconds

facts.claim: Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis describes a vital inflamed pulp unable to heal; symptoms can include lingering thermal pain, spontaneous pain and referred pain, while percussion can still be normal.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; an exact lingering-time threshold is not universal and should not be keyed without a named source.

facts.claim: Asymptomatic irreversible pulpitis is a clinical category with no reported symptoms and often normal thermal responses despite objective deep caries or likely pulp exposure.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; absence of symptoms does not establish pulpal health when objective findings indicate advanced disease.

facts.claim: Pulp necrosis is death of the pulp and usually gives no response to cold or EPT; apical symptoms require a separate apical diagnosis.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; trauma, calcification and test technique can produce false negative sensibility results.

facts.claim: Previously treated means endodontic canals have been obturated with filling material; the tooth typically does not respond to cold or electric pulp tests.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; evaluate the apical status separately and do not use a pulp test to infer the quality of the prior treatment.

facts.claim: Previously initiated therapy means partial endodontic treatment has already begun, such as pulpotomy or pulpectomy; pulp-test responses depend on what treatment was done.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; record prior treatment details because response interpretation varies with the remaining pulp.

facts.claim: Normal apical tissues are not tender to percussion or palpation; the lamina dura is intact and the periodontal ligament space is uniform.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; compare percussion and palpation with baseline control teeth.

facts.claim: Symptomatic apical periodontitis produces pain to biting, percussion or palpation; radiographs may show a normal-width ligament space early or a periapical radiolucency later.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; the radiographic appearance depends on stage and projection.

facts.claim: Asymptomatic apical periodontitis is a pulpal-origin apical lesion that appears as a periapical radiolucency without pain to percussion or palpation.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; confirm that the finding is apical and evaluate nonendodontic radiolucent differentials.

facts.claim: Acute apical abscess has rapid onset, spontaneous pain, tenderness to pressure, pus and swelling; early cases may lack a visible radiographic lesion.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; assess systemic involvement, airway risk and spread, and provide urgent source control.

facts.claim: Chronic apical abscess often has gradual onset, little discomfort and intermittent drainage through a sinus tract; a gutta-percha cone can be used radiographically to trace the tract's source.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; sinus tract origin must be confirmed because a periodontal source can mimic an endodontic tract.

facts.claim: Condensing osteitis is a localized diffuse radiopacity around a root apex associated with a low-grade inflammatory stimulus.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; the radiopacity requires a differential diagnosis and is not itself a pulpal diagnosis.

facts.claim: An incomplete cracked tooth can cause sharp pain on chewing, especially when pressure is released, and may be sensitive to cold while retaining a vital pulp.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; symptoms vary with crack direction, depth and pulpal involvement.

facts.claim: Bite testing can reproduce cusp-specific pain in a cracked tooth; transillumination can help reveal a crack because the fracture interrupts light transmission.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; neither result alone establishes crack depth or restorability.

cites.quote: important aid in locating the crack

facts.claim: A narrow isolated periodontal probing defect can indicate a crack extending below the gingiva; an isolated deep pocket raises concern for a split tooth or vertical root fracture.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; distinguish a fracture defect from periodontal disease and a draining sinus tract.

facts.claim: Vertical root fracture may produce a narrow deep pocket, sinus tract, tenderness, localized swelling or a halo/J-shaped radiolucency; early fractures can be radiographically occult.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; CBCT can also miss a fracture and is affected by filling-material artifacts.

cites.quote: a deep probing depth has been found corresponding to the root fracture line

facts.claim: A confirmed vertical root fracture in a single-rooted tooth often makes the tooth nonrestorable; management may require extraction, while selected multirooted teeth may be considered for root resection.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; prognosis depends on fracture location, tooth anatomy, periodontal support and restorability; refer complex cases.

facts.claim: Pain perceived in one tooth can be referred from another tooth or an orofacial structure, so location reported by the patient may not identify the source.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; do not perform irreversible treatment without converging diagnostic findings.

cites.quote: pain felt in one tooth may be referred

facts.claim: Trigeminal neuralgia can mimic toothache; brief electric or shock-like episodes triggered by light touch or routine movement and an inconclusive dental exam should prompt a neurologic pain differential.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; refer suspected neuralgia for medical evaluation rather than initiate irreversible dental treatment.

facts.claim: Burning mouth syndrome is a nonodontogenic pain condition that can be mistaken for dental disease when the oral examination does not reveal a tooth-based cause.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; exclude local, medication-related and systemic causes and refer when indicated.

facts.claim: Odontogenic maxillary sinusitis can present with unilateral maxillary pressure or toothache; endodontic testing and sinus findings must be considered together.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; this differential does not establish sinusitis or justify endodontic treatment without dental evidence.

facts.claim: AAE vital pulp therapy includes indirect and direct pulp capping and partial or complete pulpotomy to preserve pulp vitality after caries, trauma or restorative exposure.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; eligibility depends on examination of the exposed pulp, restorability, asepsis and the patient's circumstances.

cites.quote: direct pulp capping, and partial or complete pulpotomy

facts.claim: Indirect pulp capping places a protective material over deep dentin without exposing the pulp; the treatment aims to maintain pulp vitality under a sealed restoration.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; use the cited glossary definition and current caries-management guidance before keying treatment selection.

facts.claim: Direct pulp capping places a biocompatible material directly over a small pulp exposure when the pulp is suitable for preservation.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; case selection, contamination, hemostasis and definitive restoration affect the decision and prognosis.

facts.claim: A partial pulpotomy removes a limited superficial portion of exposed coronal pulp; a complete pulpotomy removes coronal pulp while retaining radicular pulp.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; do not infer eligibility from a diagnostic label alone; assess tissue appearance and ability to achieve hemostasis.

facts.claim: AAE describes sodium hypochlorite as an antimicrobial solution used during vital pulp therapy for hemostasis and disinfection at the dentin-pulp interface; hemostasis time is commonly 5 to 10 minutes in the statement.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; the position statement notes that recommended time may vary; use clinical judgment and a safe technique.

cites.quote: hemostasis for the pulp tissue is typically achieved

facts.claim: Calcium silicate cements, including MTA, are contemporary vital pulp therapy materials; the AAE statement reports favorable short-term results in selected permanent teeth with pulpitis.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; the reported study ranges are not a guarantee for an individual case and long-term comparative evidence is limited.

cites.loc: Use of Contemporary Materials in VPT
cites.quote: MTA is one of many tricalcium silicates

facts.claim: Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis is managed with definitive local dental treatment for pain, such as appropriate vital pulp therapy, pulpotomy/pulpectomy, root canal treatment or extraction based on diagnosis and restorability; antibiotics do not treat inflamed vital pulp.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; treatment choice requires examination, informed consent and patient-specific assessment.

facts.claim: For a localized acute apical abscess, urgent source control is canal debridement and drainage when indicated; systemic antibiotics are not a substitute for local treatment.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; spreading infection or systemic involvement changes management and urgency.

facts.claim: AAE states adjunctive antibiotics are not effective for irreversible pulpitis, symptomatic apical periodontitis or localized acute apical abscess once adequate local debridement and drainage have been achieved.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; this guidance does not cover every immune status or spreading infection scenario.

cites.quote: not effective in preventing or ameliorating signs and symptoms

facts.claim: AAE reserves therapeutic systemic antibiotics as an adjunct for endodontic infection with systemic involvement, after endodontic disinfection and drainage of swelling when present.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; the statement also discusses immunocompromise and prophylaxis as separate contexts; do not collapse them into routine treatment.

facts.claim: Trismus, dyspnea or dysphagia with an odontogenic infection can signal spread into deep fascial spaces and warrants urgent escalation for airway and medical assessment.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; emergency response depends on the patient's presentation and local protocols.

cites.loc: Signs and Symptoms Possible Condition Management Strategies

facts.claim: When antibiotics are indicated as an adjunct, AAE advises the shortest effective course, minimizing broad-spectrum use and monitoring the patient closely.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; no antibiotic selection or dose is provided here; follow current guidance and patient-specific contraindications.

facts.claim: Permanent tooth canal counts are tooth-specific patterns rather than fixed rules; anatomy reviews report variations in roots, canal number, canal merging and apical exits across tooth types and populations.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; quote points to an anatomy table; any percentage must name the study population and imaging method.

cites.quote: Number of canals per tooth in the maxilla and mandible by tooth

facts.claim: Mandibular incisors and canines usually have one root and one canal, but a second canal is more common in lateral incisors than central incisors; mandibular canines can rarely have two roots.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; prevalence varies by population and detection method; search for a second canal when findings suggest one.

cites.quote: percentage of second canals is higher in lateral incisors

facts.claim: Maxillary first premolars commonly have two canals, while maxillary second premolars more often have one; a single root does not guarantee a single canal.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; anatomy varies by population, tooth and method; confirm each canal clinically and radiographically.

cites.quote: maxillary PM1s predominantly possess double roots and double canals, whereas maxillary PM2s and mandibular PMs were primarily characterized by single-rooted with a single canal

facts.claim: Mandibular first premolars are often single-rooted but have a clinically important chance of canal bifurcation; mandibular second premolars are more often single-canal but can vary.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; population reviews report different frequencies; do not apply a pooled percentage to an unnamed population.

cites.quote: first premolar was more prone to bifurcation of canals

facts.claim: Maxillary first molars usually have three roots and three or four canals; the second mesiobuccal canal is common enough that it should be actively sought.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; the cited 2022 CBCT review's prevalence estimate depends on its included populations and imaging method.

cites.quote: 68.2% of maxillary first molars had a second MB canal

facts.claim: A second mesiobuccal canal is also found in maxillary second molars, with reported prevalence varying by study and population.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; reported frequency depends on population and detection technique; do not assume a universal percentage.

cites.quote: 22% of MB2 canals in maxillary second molars

facts.claim: Mandibular first molars commonly have two roots, with two canals in the mesial root and one or two in the distal root; an extra distal canal is a reason to inspect the chamber floor carefully.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; canal counts vary, including extra roots and canals; access must preserve tooth structure.

cites.quote: number of canals in the 3D reconstructed images

facts.claim: Mandibular second molars often have two mesial canals and one distal canal, but canal number ranges widely and C-shaped anatomy is a recognized variation.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; this systematic review included broad anatomical variation; do not key an exact count as invariant.

cites.quote: number of canals ranged from 1 to 5

facts.claim: Working length is the distance from a coronal reference point to the point at which canal preparation and obturation should end, usually near the apical constriction.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; the constriction and foramen positions vary; do not use a radiographic apex as an exact anatomical endpoint.

cites.quote: point of termination for the preparation and obturation

facts.claim: An electronic apex locator helps estimate working length, while radiographs assess root morphology, file position and treatment progress; using both can reduce error.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; EAL readings can be inconsistent in open apices, resorption and complex anatomy.

cites.quote: working length determination in conjunction with electronic apex locators

facts.claim: Sodium hypochlorite is used for antimicrobial action and dissolution of organic tissue; extrusion beyond the canal can injure periapical tissues.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; concentration and exposure affect toxicity; prevent extrusion with a loose-fitting needle, controlled pressure and safe depth.

cites.quote: NaOCl can dissolve organic components and eliminate bacteria

facts.claim: EDTA chelates calcium and removes inorganic debris and the smear layer; it does not provide the organic tissue dissolution function of sodium hypochlorite.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; prolonged exposure can soften dentin; do not mix directly with sodium hypochlorite because it reduces available chlorine.

facts.claim: Chlorhexidine provides antimicrobial activity but cannot dissolve tissue or remove the smear layer, so it does not replace sodium hypochlorite and EDTA.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; avoid direct NaOCl-CHX contact because the combination forms a precipitate; rinse between solutions if used sequentially.

facts.claim: Extruded sodium hypochlorite can cause chemical injury and periapical tissue damage; prevention focuses on controlled delivery that avoids binding or forcing irrigant past the apex.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; this fact is not an emergency-treatment protocol; promptly assess and manage a suspected accident with appropriate specialist support.

facts.claim: Gutta-percha is a common solid core material for root canal obturation and is used with a sealer to fill the prepared canal system.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; no obturation technique has been shown to compensate for inadequate cleaning, length control or coronal seal.

facts.claim: Root resorption is classified by location as internal or external; pathologic external types include surface, inflammatory, replacement and cervical resorption.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; classification names differ across systems; use the named classification when testing subtype terminology.

cites.quote: loss of dental hard tissue because of odontoclastic action

facts.claim: Internal inflammatory resorption begins on the canal wall after loss of predentin protection; external inflammatory resorption begins on the root surface and is sustained by infection.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; resorption diagnosis and treatment depend on extent, vitality, infection and restorability.

facts.claim: Internal resorption tends to enlarge the canal space, while external resorption is centered on the root surface; angled radiographs can help distinguish their apparent relationship to the canal.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; two-dimensional imaging can be inconclusive and CBCT is considered only when it will change management.

facts.claim: After a luxation injury, early pulp sensibility tests may be falsely negative; IADT recommends serial follow-up and does not support root canal treatment solely because of one negative response.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; this summary applies to permanent teeth and the IADT 2020 guideline; injury type and root maturity change follow-up.

cites.loc: Pulp status evaluation: sensibility and vitality testing
cites.quote: lack of a response to pulp sensi- bility testing is not conclusive

facts.claim: For a replanted avulsed permanent tooth with a closed apex, IADT recommends initiating root canal treatment within two weeks after replantation.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; this is an endodontic component of IADT 2020 avulsion guidance, not a general dental avulsion protocol.

cites.quote: Initiate root canal treatment within 2 weeks

facts.claim: For an avulsed permanent tooth with an open apex, spontaneous pulp-space revascularization may occur; avoid root canal treatment unless follow-up shows pulp necrosis and infection.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; monitor for inflammatory root resorption and treat promptly if necrosis/infection is diagnosed.

cites.quote: root canal treatment should be avoided unless

facts.claim: For immature permanent teeth, traumatic pulp exposures can be treated with conservative pulp therapies such as pulp capping or partial pulpotomy to preserve pulp and allow continued root development.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; choose therapy after assessing pulp status, exposure, root maturity, restorability and ability to provide follow-up.

cites.loc: Pulp preservation in immature permanent teeth

facts.claim: A missed canal may retain pulp tissue or infection and is a recognized cause of persistent disease after root canal treatment.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; evaluate anatomy and prior treatment before attributing a persistent lesion to a missed canal.

facts.claim: Ledges, canal transportation and perforations can compromise cleaning and sealing; technically complex procedural errors are appropriate reasons for endodontic specialist referral.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; outcomes depend on defect location, remaining tooth structure and ability to manage the error.

facts.claim: A separated instrument does not automatically make a tooth hopeless; management considers infection, canal anatomy, fragment location, bypass/removal risk and the overall prognosis.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; do not recommend instrument removal without considering perforation, dentin loss and referral.

facts.claim: Endodontic outcomes should include tooth survival, pain, infection signs, radiographic healing or maintained health, function, retreatment and adverse events.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; these are standardized outcome domains, not a guarantee that every study reports each measure.

cites.loc: What Outcomes Made the Core List?
cites.quote: tooth survival, pain, signs of infection

facts.claim: Follow-up evaluates symptoms, sinus tract, percussion/palpation, function, restoration integrity and serial periapical healing; an asymptomatic tooth can still require radiographic review.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; follow-up interval depends on initial disease, treatment and current guidance.

facts.claim: Persistent disease after root canal treatment does not automatically require extraction; reassess the cause and consider nonsurgical retreatment, surgery, referral or extraction based on prognosis and patient preference.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; treatment decisions require restorability, periodontal status, fracture assessment, anatomy and informed consent.

facts.claim: Adequate coronal restoration and root canal treatment quality are both associated with periapical healing; a leaking or failed restoration can undermine an otherwise adequate canal treatment.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; the cited review reports observational evidence and does not establish a single restoration design for every tooth.

cites.quote: healing of apical periodontitis increase with both

facts.claim: Plan the definitive restoration with endodontic treatment; preserve remaining tooth structure and provide a durable coronal seal, with cuspal coverage considered when structural loss makes fracture risk higher.
facts.conditions: Not independently checked; restoration choice depends on tooth type, remaining walls, cracks, occlusion and patient-specific factors.
